title: One to Many Relationships
summary: Covers the one to many (equivalently many to one) relationship using student and homework_submission tables, where the 'many' table carries a foreign key to the 'one' table. Shows joining the two and narrowing the selected columns.

concepts.heading: One to many vs many to one
points: One row on one side relates to many rows on the other: one student has many homework submissions; one customer has many orders.
The direction depends on the starting table: from student it is one to many; from homework_submission it is many to one. It is the same relationship.
Each submission belongs to exactly one student (no group work in this example).
In crow's-foot diagrams the 'many' end has the three-pronged foot touching the foreign key field, the 'one' end attaches to the primary key.

concepts.heading: Where the keys live
points: The many-side table gets its own primary key (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY) because every submission must be uniquely identifiable.
It also gets a foreign key column (student_id) storing the id of the owning student. No UNIQUE here, so the same student id can repeat, which is what makes it one to many.
Compared with one to one: the only structural difference is dropping UNIQUE and giving the child table its own id.

concepts.heading: Creating the table
points: homework_submission has three fields: id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, mark INTEGER, student_id INTEGER REFERENCES student(id).
student_id is INTEGER so it matches the type of student.id; REFERENCES student(id) names the table and column it points to and makes it a foreign key.
Real schemas would add more columns (date, class, teacher); this one is kept minimal.

concepts.heading: Naming convention
points: Singular (student) or plural (students) table names are both acceptable. Follow the team's rule and stay consistent, never mix them.

concepts.heading: Inserting data
points: Only mark and student_id are supplied; id is auto-generated 1, 2, 3 by SERIAL.
One INSERT can add several rows by listing multiple value tuples separated by commas: (98, 1), (87, 1), (88, 1). All three belong to student 1.
Viewing homework_submission alone shows only numeric student ids, which are hard to read, hence the join.

concepts.heading: Joining
points: SELECT * FROM student JOIN homework_submission ON student.id = homework_submission.student_id returns one row per submission with the student's details repeated on each.
Qualifying the column (table.column) is clearer; unqualified student_id works only because the name exists in just one table.
Narrow the output by listing columns instead of *: SELECT student.id, first_name, last_name, mark. id must be qualified because both tables have it; the other names are unique so need no prefix.
Table order after FROM does not change the matched set for an inner join.

task.name: Add homework_submission and write the join yourself
task.starting_point: school database from the previous lesson with student and contact_detail; queries.sql from the resources.
task.goal: Create the many-side table, insert three submissions for student 1, then write the join before looking at the answer.
steps: Run CREATE TABLE homework_submission and refresh to see it.
Run the INSERT with three (mark, student_id) tuples.
View the table to see the raw ids.
Write a query joining student to homework_submission on the matching id, without peeking at queries.sql.
Narrow it to student.id, first_name, last_name and mark.
task.expected_result: Three rows, one per submission, each showing Angela Yu with marks 98, 87 and 88.

solution_code.code:
SELECT student.id, first_name, last_name, mark
FROM student
JOIN homework_submission
ON student.id = student_id

task.reference_repo_path: Section 33 - PostgreSQL/33.12 - One to Many Relationships/queries.sql

pitfalls: Adding UNIQUE to the foreign key turns it into one to one.
Selecting id without a table prefix gives an ambiguous column error.
Inventing a student_id that does not exist in student causes a foreign key violation.
Mixing singular and plural table names.
